---
title: "09 · Practice — Formal Power Series"
---

The three solved exercises each attack one contract from the chapter:
normalization before a logarithm, coefficients that are invisible at a given
precision, and reading a convolution as a product you can divide by. Do them
before the contest problem — they are small enough to finish on paper.

## Solved exercises

### A. Normalize before taking logarithms

Over the rationals, find the normalized logarithm of $A=2+2x$ through degree
three. What is its exponential?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The logarithmic derivative ignores a constant multiplicative factor.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$A'/A=1/(1+x)=1-x+x^2+\cdots$, so normalized $\log A=x-x^2/2+x^3/3$.
Its exponential is $1+x\pmod{x^4}$, not $2+2x$. Recovering $A$ requires
remembering its constant factor separately.
:::

### B. Invisible coefficients

How many roots does $B^2=0\pmod{x^5}$ have over $\mathbb F_5$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Use the first nonzero coefficient rather than solving five equations.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A nonzero square has valuation twice the valuation of its root, so
$v(B)\ge3$. Precisely the polynomials $b_3x^3+b_4x^4$ work, giving $5^2=25$
roots including zero. This count is in the truncated ring, not the infinite
domain $\mathbb F_5[[x]]$.
:::

### C. Undo a first-occurrence convolution

Suppose events observed at time $n$ split uniquely by their first occurrence:
$g_n=\sum_{i=0}^nf_i h_{n-i}$ with $h_0=1$.
Given $G=1/(1-2x)$ and $H=1/(1-x)$, find all $f_n$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Interpret the convolution as a product before selecting an FPS operation.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$FH=G$ and $H$ is a unit, so $F=(1-x)/(1-2x)$.
Thus $f_0=1$, and for $n\ge1$, $f_n=2^n-2^{n-1}=2^{n-1}$.
The decomposition must be unique; allowing several candidate first occurrences
would overcount and invalidate the product equation. For arbitrary prefixes,
one inverse and one convolution compute the answer in $O(M(n))$.
:::

## 1. AtCoder ABC 289 Ex — Trio (`Advanced`)

- [Statement](https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc289/tasks/abc289_h) ·
  [official editorial](https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc289/editorial/5728) · English/Japanese
- Train: first-occurrence recurrence becomes FPS division/inversion.
- Prerequisites: [probability and conditioning](../12-probability/chapter.qmd)
  and [generating functions](../10-generating-functions/chapter.qmd); return here
  after those concepts. The official editorial also derives the all-meeting
  probability via convolution, including negative-index offsets.

<details><summary>Hint 1</summary>Count meetings at time $t$ without requiring that it is the first meeting.</details>
<details><summary>Hint 2</summary>Decompose by the first meeting time; this is a convolution.</details>
<details><summary>Hint 3</summary>Translate the recurrence to a product of generating functions and divide.</details>
